Strengths: the design is clean. Commands are functions that return the output string, and main() does the I/O and maps CliError to an exit code via process.exitCode (todo.mjs:106-122). Arguments are checked before any file I/O, so usage-type errors do not depend on file state, and a test covers that (test:249-256). Writes are skipped when nothing changes: `done` on an already-done todo and `clear-done` with 0 do not rewrite or create the file (todo.mjs:84, 101). The tests are well organized by command with exact {code, stdout, stderr} checks. They cover sort with out-of-order data, removing everything then adding, toString as a command, all five commands on a corrupt file, valid JSON with the wrong shape, the default cwd path, TODO_FILE, and no leftover temp files. The README is thorough and accurate: a Node 18+ requirement, a storage section, and an exit-code table that lists each message. Defects: errors that are not CliError (EISDIR, a missing parent dir, a todos entry of null) are rethrown and print raw stack traces (todo.mjs:116; probed). save() does not remove the temp file if the write or rename fails (todo.mjs:46-50). It reads '-1' as an invalid id (exit 2), though the spec's 'non-integer' wording suggests not found; that reading is defensible. The 'corrupt data file' error is built in two places in load().

reasoning: All three meet the spec's core behaviour and pass their own tests, so the ranking comes from edge cases, design, tests and robustness. Z and X are close. Z wins on design: its commands are pure functions that return strings, it checks arguments before any file I/O, it skips writes when nothing changes, its README is the most complete, and its test suite is broad and well organized, including checks on argument precedence and structurally bad JSON. X wins on error handling: it catches every error with a friendly message, removes the temp file when a write fails, and has the most thorough corrupt-file test matrix. It also reads the spec more literally on negative ids. Against that, X loads the data file before checking arguments, mixes output into the command logic, rewrites the file on no-op commands, has a usage text that names the wrong program, and uses a test glob that needs a newer Node on Windows. On balance Z's structure and docs edge out X's error handling, and the difference is about half a point. Y is clearly third. It is correct on the main paths, but it rejects valid JSON that lacks lastId as corrupt, and it can assign a duplicate id when the counter is stale, because lastId is never checked against existing ids. It prints stack traces on I/O errors. Its test suite is the thinnest: no sort, default-path or structural-corruption tests, and it leaks temp dirs. Its README is also the sparsest.

Object.hasOwn rejects prototype names such as __proto__ and toString.

Defects:
- Storage schema is brittle (todo.mjs:38). It requires an integer `lastId`, so a hand-written `{"todos":[...]}` is reported as corrupt.

Y.notes:
All 75 own tests pass. It meets the spec fully for CLI use.

Strengths:
- The data file's shape is validated, and valid JSON with the wrong shape is also treated as corrupt (todo.mjs:33-38).
- nextId is computed as max(nextId, maxId+1), so ids stay unique even if the file is out of sync.
- The temp file goes in the same folder and is renamed over the data file, and it is removed if the write fails (todo.mjs:43-52).
- An already-done `done` and a zero-count `clear-done` do not rewrite the file, which avoids needless writes.
- Unexpected errors become `Error: <msg>` with exit 1 (todo.mjs:120) instead of a stack trace.

A README quick-start replay test is included.

Defects:
- nextId sanitization is weak (todo.mjs:40). `Number(data.nextId) || 1` accepts fractional or string values, so `{"nextId":"3.5","todos":[]}` gives `Added #3.5`. This only happens with a tampered file.

- The README is clear and accurate but does not mention that I/O failures exit 1.

Z.notes:
All 17 own tests pass. Every spec line is met, and my extra probes (-1, 01, +1, ' 1', 1e2, a huge id, an empty file, [], {}, null items, prototype-name commands, unicode text, a missing directory, a directory as TODO_FILE) all behaved sensibly.

Strengths:

- Schema validation includes the todo items, and nextId is checked with Number.isInteger and combined as max(nextId, maxId+1) (todo.mjs:24-48).

- File-system errors are wrapped as friendly `Error: cannot read/write data file` messages with exit 1, instead of stack traces.

Exact stdout/stderr/status are checked through deepEqual.

Minor issues:

- The tests cover fewer corrupt shapes than Y's (2 against 7).
- There is no test for a not-found id of 0 or a negative id.

Y comes second. Its code is equally clean, with an atomic ON CONFLICT insert, good tests (a chunked-413 case, raw-socket traversal requests, app.js run end to end against the real server) and the best README. It loses points for the Location 500 bug and for not counting 429-rejected POSTs toward the window, which is arguably against 'every POST counts'. X is last. It is functionally correct and has a nice testable createApp factory, but it shares the Location 500 bug, has an unpruned and unbounded limiter, decodes the whole path before routing, and has the thinnest tests (no frontend rendering tests, little edge coverage), plus a minimal UI and README.

X.notes: Own suite: 27/27 pass. Black-box probe (spawned `node server.mjs` with PORT/DB_FILE/ADMIN_TOKEN) passed every check: prints listening; DB created; default PORT 3000 and ./data.db in cwd; 201 shape with short=http://localhost:<port>/<code>; 409; 415 with missing or text/plain CT, mixed-case CT with charset accepted; 413 with Content-Length and with chunked body (server stays up); exactly 10240 bytes accepted; 400 for bad JSON, null/array/string/number bodies, ftp/javascript/mailto/data/file/relative/'http://'/2049-char URLs, bad codes incl. 3/32/33 boundaries and non-string; stats shape with numeric clicks and ISO createdAt; 302 plus click count; DELETE 401/401/404/204 with token checked before the 404, always 401 when the token is unset or empty; GET /, /app.js content types; traversal (encoded ../, backslash, NUL, drive letter) blocked; 20 mixed rejected POSTs then 429 JSON, GET/DELETE not limited; data persists across restart. Strengths: createApp factory with DI (server.mjs:212); clean HttpError flow; redirect normalises Location via new URL().href so non-ASCII and IDN targets work (server.mjs:255); rejects control chars in URLs (server.mjs:141); rate limiter keeps at most 20 stamps per IP plus a periodic sweep (server.mjs:69-89); length-checked timingSafeEqual; WAL and busy_timeout. Frontend app.js exports pure fetch helpers and render helpers built only with createElement/textContent, and links only http(s) URLs. Tests are strong: a fake DOM that throws on innerHTML checks the render functions, there are fetch-logic error-mapping tests, traversal tests, a rate-limit test that includes rejected POSTs, a non-ASCII redirect regression test and a spawned-process env test. Minor: HEAD /<code> counts a click (server.mjs:248); static lookup does a statSync before every redirect; 'http:example.com' is accepted (all three do this); README says `npm test # runs: node --test` but the script is `node --test test/*.test.mjs`; no chunked-413 test.

Y.notes: Own suite: 66/66 pass (many are parameterized cases). The black-box probe passed every spec check, the same set X passed, including chunked 413, non-ASCII, latin1 and IDN redirects via new URL().href (server.mjs:203), traversal blocking, unset/empty ADMIN_TOKEN giving 401, rate limit with rejected POSTs counted, persistence, and default PORT and DB. Strengths: security headers (nosniff, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy) and an Allow header on 405 (server.mjs:270-297); SHA-256 then timingSafeEqual token compare that does not leak length; clear routing where static files are served only for dotted paths, so they can never collide with codes (server.mjs:257); graceful SIGINT/SIGTERM shutdown. Tests spawn the real process (truly black box, which also checks the listening message) and cover 415 with no CT, 413, invalid JSON/array, URL and code boundaries, 409, stats keys, the redirect click count, a non-ASCII Location, delete flows, traversal, unset token, and a rate limit that mixes failing POSTs. Frontend fetch helpers are tested thoroughly (network failure, non-JSON body, missing error field) and isSafeHref is tested with many cases. Weaknesses: the module has top-level side effects (opens the DB and listens on import), so it cannot be imported in-process (server.mjs:33, 299). Static serving is limited to an 8-entry MIME whitelist and to paths containing '.', so other public/ files (e.g. .webp, .xml, extensionless) return 404, a partial miss on 'other files under public/ are served' (server.mjs:217-220). HEAD returns 405. The per-IP rate-limit array is unbounded within the window and is re-filtered on each request (server.mjs:77-83). PORT='' becomes port 0. Render functions are not exported or tested (init(doc) is exported but unused in tests); only a static regex check for innerHTML. The CRLF-containing URL is accepted (it is safely normalised on redirect). No .gitignore for data.db. The README is the best of the three: bash and PowerShell config examples, an API table, curl examples, a layout section.

Z.notes: Own suite: 18/18 pass. The black-box probe passed most spec checks: 201/409/415/413 (including chunked)/400 cases, stats, 302 plus clicks, DELETE semantics, unset token, rate limit including rejected POSTs, static content types, traversal, persistence, defaults. Defects: the redirect writes the raw stored URL into Location (server.mjs:219). For a valid non-ASCII URL such as https://example.com/€ or an IDN host, writeHead throws ERR_INVALID_CHAR, so GET /<code> returns 500 instead of 302. The click has already been incremented by the UPDATE...RETURNING before the failure, so clicks are counted for failed redirects. Latin-1 characters (café) are sent as raw latin1 bytes rather than percent-encoded. A URL containing CR/LF passes validation (the WHATWG parser strips them) and is stored, then the redirect 500s. The 409 detection relies on the substring String(err.message).includes('UNIQUE') (server.mjs:175), which is fragile. The per-IP rate-limit arrays are unbounded within the window, and cleanup runs only when there are more than 10k IPs (server.mjs:60-73). Handlers mix `return sendJson` and `throw HttpError` styles. HEAD /<code> counts a click. DB_FILE='' gives an anonymous temporary DB (?? instead of ||). Strengths: compact startServer factory with an injectable port, dbFile, adminToken and rateLimit; hashed timingSafeEqual; nosniff and CSP on static files; import.meta.main entry. Tests are thinner. The most important gap is that there is no non-ASCII redirect test, so the bug above goes undetected. The traversal assertion uses fetch, which normalises %2e%2e, so it does not exercise traversal; there is no 415-without-CT test, and most API tests run with rateLimit: Infinity on :memory:. The frontend tests cover only the fetch helpers (5 tests) plus a regex sink check. The DOM code uses the global document and cannot be unit-tested. The README is accurate and concise but has no curl examples or detailed status table.

reasoning: X and Y are both spec-complete. Each passed every check in a black-box probe of about 70 checks, run against the spawned server: content-type/size/JSON/url/code validation with boundaries, 409, stats shape, redirect plus click counting including non-ASCII/IDN targets, DELETE token semantics, static serving and traversal, the 20-per-60s rate limit counting rejected POSTs, persistence and env defaults. X edges out Y on engineering and test depth. X's server is an importable createApp factory. Its rate limiter is bounded per IP. It rejects control characters at input. Its tests also verify the DOM rendering path using a fake DOM that throws on innerHTML, plus a spawned-process env test. Y is a module with import-time side effects. Its static serving drops files outside a small MIME whitelist or without a dot, and its rendering is checked only by a regex. Y does have stronger docs and extra security headers. Z ranks last because of a real correctness bug: it puts the raw stored URL in the Location header, so valid non-ASCII/IDN URLs (and CRLF-containing ones its validator accepts) produce a 500 on redirect while still counting a click. It also has a fragile message-substring 409 check and an unbounded limiter. Its tests are notably thinner and miss that bug; its traversal test is ineffective because fetch normalises the path.

X.notes:
Own suite: 27/27 pass. I ran black-box probes against `node server.mjs`. Almost everything passes: 415 (missing or wrong content type, charset allowed), 413 (both Content-Length and chunked bodies), 400 (bad JSON, null, array, or empty body), the URL and code boundary cases (2048/2049 chars, codes of 3 and 32 chars), 409, the rate limit (20 mixed rejected POSTs, then 429; X-Forwarded-For does not bypass it; GETs are not limited), DELETE returning 401, 404 or 204 (always 401 when ADMIN_TOKEN is unset or empty), static files, path traversal, and persistence across a restart.

Defects:
(1) server.mjs:300 `Number(process.env.PORT) || 3000` turns PORT=0 into 3000. A harness that uses PORT=0 and parses the 'listening on' line would bind the fixed port 3000 and collide.
(2) server.mjs:255 sets Location to `new URL(row.url).href`, not the stored url. 'https://example.com' redirects to 'https://example.com/', and 'HTTPS://Example.COM/Path?q=a b' redirects to a lowercased, percent-encoded form. The spec says Location is the stored url.
(3) tokenMatches (server.mjs:180-185) leaks the token length before calling timingSafeEqual. Minor.
(4) README says `npm test # runs: node --test`, but package.json runs `node --test test/*.test.mjs`.
(5) HEAD /<code> counts as a click.

Strengths:
- isHttpUrl (server.mjs:141) rejects control characters, so CRLF URLs never get stored.
- Non-ASCII URLs redirect safely, and the click is counted only after the Location is computed (server.mjs:254-256).
- The createApp factory is injectable for in-process tests. WAL mode and busy_timeout are set. Body draining and Connection: close on 413 are correct.
- Frontend: render functions are exported and tested against a fake DOM whose innerHTML, outerHTML and insertAdjacentHTML setters throw. This directly verifies the textContent requirement and javascript: link suppression. Strongest frontend tests of the three.
- API tests cover CRLF, non-ASCII, missing content type, many traversal variants, and the env vars on a spawned server.

Y.notes:
Own suite: 66/66 pass (many parametrized cases). Black-box probes pass for everything the spec lists except the redirect Location. That covers 415/413 (Content-Length and chunked)/400 handling, the URL and code boundaries, 409, the rate limit with mixed rejected POSTs (no X-Forwarded-For bypass), DELETE semantics including unset or empty ADMIN_TOKEN, PORT=0, static files, path traversal, and persistence.

Defects:
(1) server.mjs:203 sends `new URL(row.url).href` as Location instead of the stored url. 'https://example.com' becomes 'https://example.com/', and mixed-case or space-containing URLs get rewritten. This deviates from the spec on a very common input.
(2) The whole server lives at module level (DB opened and listen() called on import, server.mjs:33,299). It cannot be imported for in-process tests or reuse.
(3) The routing heuristic `segment.includes('.')` decides what counts as a static file (server.mjs:257), and allowFor (server.mjs:292) duplicates the routing table. Extensionless public files and unknown MIME types return 404.
(4) HEAD on / returns 405.
(5) URLs containing CRLF are accepted and stored raw. The redirect neutralizes them, but they come back raw in the API responses.
(6) test/helpers/server.mjs is picked up by `node --test` as a test file. Harmless noise.

Strengths:
- Non-ASCII Location is safe. Token comparison is timing-safe via hashing.
- Security headers on all responses (nosniff, X-Frame-Options, Referrer-Policy), plus an Allow header on 405.
- Bodies are drained correctly on 413. Graceful SIGINT/SIGTERM shutdown.
- Tests spawn the real entrypoint for every API test, and include 6 traversal variants and a charset test.
- Extensive frontend fetch-logic tests (non-JSON bodies, network failure, unreadable 200 response) and isSafeHref tests. The DOM rendering itself is only grep-checked.
- Best README: env table, bash and PowerShell examples, curl walkthrough, project layout. All accurate.

Z.notes:
Own suite: 18/18 pass. Black-box probes: every spec check passed. That includes exact Location for 'https://example.com' and mixed-case URLs, PORT and PORT=0, the 'listening on <port>' line, DB_FILE persistence across a restart, 415 (with charset and case handling), 413 for Content-Length, chunked and 200KB bodies, a 10240-byte body accepted, 400 for invalid, null, string or empty bodies, the URL and code boundaries, 409, the rate limit with 20 mixed rejected POSTs then 429 (no X-Forwarded-For bypass, GETs not limited), DELETE returning 401, 404 or 204 (always 401 when ADMIN_TOKEN is unset or empty), static content types, and path traversal.

Defects:
(1) server.mjs:219 writes the raw stored url into Location. URLs that pass validation but are not valid header values ('https://例え.jp/ü', or a URL containing CRLF) return a 500 at redirect time, after clicks has already been incremented. isValidUrl (server.mjs:96) does not reject control characters.
(2) HEAD /<code> increments clicks.
(3) The code-pattern check runs before static lookup (server.mjs:216), so an extensionless public file could never be served. Not an issue today.
(4) Tests are fewer and lean on the happy path. There is no chunked-413 test, no missing-content-type test, and only one traversal case. Frontend tests cover only the fetch helpers plus an innerHTML grep; DOM rendering is not exercised.

Strengths:
- Smallest and clearest server (247 lines). startServer({port, dbFile, adminToken, rateLimit}) is injectable, so tests run in-process on :memory: and a spawn test checks env handling, persistence and the listening line.
- Rate-limit check runs before content-type and body checks, so every POST counts.
- Timing-safe hashed token comparison.
- Static files get CSP and nosniff headers. Body draining is correct.
- Frontend is minimal and correct: textContent and replaceChildren only, with a separate style.css that exercises 'other public files'.
- README is concise and accurate.

reasoning:
All three pass their own suites and nearly every black-box probe. They differ on a few spec deviations I found by running them.

Z is the only one that sets Location to the stored url exactly as the spec says. X and Y both normalize it through `new URL().href`, so 'https://example.com' redirects to 'https://example.com/'. That breaks the spec on the most common kind of test input.

Z's main flaw is narrower: URLs that are not valid header values (non-ASCII IRIs, or URLs containing CRLF) are accepted, then 500 at redirect time. That is a real robustness defect, but an edge case. Z also has the cleanest, smallest code with an injectable server, so it ranks first even though its tests are thinner.

Y vs X:
- Both share the Location deviation.
- X adds a second one: PORT=0 falls back to 3000 (`Number(PORT) || 3000`), which breaks harnesses that request an ephemeral port.
- X has the better architecture (an injectable createApp) and the better frontend tests (a fake DOM that fails if innerHTML is used). It is also the only solution that rejects control characters in URLs.
- Y has the best README, security headers, and full entrypoint-level API tests, but its module-level design is weaker.

Spec compliance weighs most, so Y ranks above X.
